blocks.en: Welcome back to Michael's Morning Listening!
Today we meet a real super-sniffer with the best nose in the business.
Then we blast off to Mars, where a brave spacecraft will grab a piece of the moon Phobos.
Let's jump in!
Meet Sgiath, a six-year-old black Labrador from the Scottish Highlands.
She began as a mountain rescue dog — but today she has a different job.

Sgiath is now believed to be the first dog in the world trained to smell a dangerous sea creature — the carpet sea squirt, also known as "sea vomit." This creature came from abroad, from waters near Japan, and has spread across harbours in Britain.
It grows like a dark cloud over oyster farms and smothers the native sea life underneath.
Finding it early is important, but it is not easy.
Scientists must wear thick gloves and use DNA tests to spot it.
Sgiath needs only her nose.
Her handler, Dr. Texa Sim, says the first time Sgiath tried, she went straight to it — all by herself!
At low tide, she works with Dr. Sim along the shore.
When she finds something, she never barks — she just goes still and stares.
Her reward is food — she is a greedy girl!
All this clever nose work won Sgiath the Animal of the Year award from IFAW, the International Fund for Animal Welfare.
She shows us the true value of a great nose — and a great dog!
Now let's fly to Mars — not the planet, but one of its moons!
Japan has launched a big space mission called MMX, which stands for Martian Moons eXploration.
Its goal: bring home a piece of Phobos, the larger of Mars' two moons.
Phobos is a lumpy, potato-shaped rock about twenty-two kilometers wide — not a perfect ball at all!
Scientists still do not know where Phobos came from.
Was it a passing asteroid caught by Mars long ago?
Or was it born from the dust of a giant crash on young Mars?
The answer has been hiding behind millions of miles — until now.
MMX will spend about three years flying around Phobos.
A small robot arm will dig into the surface twice, collecting at least ten grams of dust and rocks — about the weight of a rabbit!
The landing must be as gentle as silk, because gravity on Phobos is very weak.
One wrong move, and the spacecraft could bounce right off!
Then a small capsule will house the precious samples for the long trip home.
Count the years: it is a five-year journey!
Back on Earth, the whole team will be wide awake for an exciting activity — opening the capsule and reading the story in the dust.
Those tiny grains may tell us how Mars' moons were born, and how water and life's building blocks traveled around the young solar system.
Here's today's idiom: "have a nose for something." It means you are good at finding or understanding something — like a dog with a great nose!
For example: "My friend Jack has a nose for good stories — he taught himself to write news at twelve." Jack finds stories the way Sgiath finds sea creatures!
So — do you have a nose for something?
Maybe you have a nose for music, or a nose for finding lost socks at home!
That brings us to the end of today's show!
Here's a question: If you could train a dog to smell out one thing in the world, what would you choose?
A lost toy?
Hidden treasure?
Or maybe your homework?
Have a wonderful day, and see you tomorrow morning!
